title: Co-location of skill-related suppliers: advancing coagglomeration research using firm-to-firm network data
abstract: Strong local clusters help firms compete on global markets. One explanation for this is that firms benefit from locating close to their suppliers and customers. However, the emergence of global supply chains shows that physical proximity is not necessarily a prerequisite to successfully manage customer-supplier relations anymore. This raises the question when firms need to colocate in value chains and when they can coordinate over longer distances. We hypothesize that one important aspect is the extent to which supply chain partners exchange not just goods but also know-how. We exploit detailed micro-data for the Hungarian economy between 2015 and 2017, linking firm registries, employer-employee matched data and firm-to-firm transaction data from value-added tax records. We show that supply chains are more likely to support coagglomeration when the industries involved are also skill related. That is, input-output and labor market channels reinforce each other, but supplier connections only matter for colocation when industries have similar labor requirements, suggesting that they employ similar types of know-how.
summary_en: When do firms in supply-chain relationships locate near each other, and when can they manage long-distance partnerships? Juhász, Elekes, Ilyés and Neffke link Hungarian firm-to-firm VAT transaction records (2015-2017) with employer-employee data to test whether supply-chain coagglomeration is reinforced by skill-relatedness — that is, by overlapping labour-market requirements. They find that input-output and labour-market channels reinforce each other, but supplier connections only generate co-location when the trading industries also share similar skills. Goods alone don't require proximity; know-how does.
data_used: Hungarian firm-level VAT transaction records 2015-2017 from NAV, linked to employer-employee matched data from KSH and ONYF (~all formal firms with revenue above the VAT threshold). Cross-industry skill-relatedness measures from labour-flow data.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for Hungarian regional-development policy (Ministry of Economic Development, IFKA, EU Cohesion programmes). The paper shows clusters succeed when supply-chain partners share labour-market overlap, not just product transactions. Useful for sharpening industrial-park and SEZ designation criteria — co-locate skill-related firms, not just any input-output partners.
